evidence_quotes.quote: Afin de rendre compte de cette complexité, nous montrerons, dans un premier temps, les nouveaux dispositifs institutionnels mis en place à l’échelle nationale au Burkina Faso en réponse aux préconisations internationales, dans un contexte de décentralisation. Dans un deuxième temps, nous présenterons le cadre de la Réforme du secteur de l’hydraulique, en explicitant le rôle joué par les associations d’usagers de l’eau et la difficulté à mettre en œuvre des principes participatifs pourtant au cœur de la Réforme.

La Réforme, en conformité avec le référentiel néolibéral, a retenu le principe du paiement de l’eau. Le tarif est supposé couvrir les charges d’exploitation et le renouvellement d’infrastructures à durée de vie courte puisque l’État a la charge de renouveler les infrastructures de longue durée (au-delà de 15 ans), telles que les canalisations, les châteaux d’eau, etc.

Enfin, la commune délègue la gestion des autres points d’eau qui sont sur son territoire (PMH) à des associations d’usagers de l’eau recomposées, reconduisant des principes qui restent malgré tout proches de la gestion communautaire, en corrigeant certains défauts (notamment des formes de clientélisme).

Les études de terrain ont été réalisées dans le cadre de l’ANR Sud II APPI « Une action publique éclatée. Production et institutionnalisation de l’action publique dans les secteurs de l’eau et du foncier. Bénin, Burkina Faso et Niger », 2011-2014, coordonnée par C. Baron.
Le bilan annuel 2012 du Rapport du PN-AEPA indique des taux d’accès à l’eau potable de 58,5 % en milieu rural et 80 % en milieu urbain en 2011.
Une corrélation entre fonctionnalité et modes de gestion peut être opérée. Les deux régions où les taux de fonctionnalité sont les plus élevés sont celles gérées par l’ADAE.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines drinking-water service access and rural/semi-urban hydraulic infrastructure management (handpumps/PMH, simplified piped networks/AEPS, autonomous water posts/PEA, and urban ONEA networks) in Burkina Faso.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the paper analyses national institutional, legal, decentralization, and hybrid governance reforms in Burkina Faso's drinking-water sector. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it specifically examines legal and regulatory rules directly governing service access, including tariff and cost-recovery rules (municipal council tariff-setting vs. ONEA uniform tariffs, volumetric vs. flat-rate user fees at AEPS and PMH, and informal local accommodations for poor villagers), utility/infrastructure ownership and delegation rules (Decree 2009-107 transferring municipal ownership, Decree 2000-514 mandating delegated affermage to private operators or ONEA for AEPS vs. licensed Water Users Associations/AUEs for PMH, and ONEA profitability/parceled-zone extension conditions), and statutory licensing/composition rules for AUEs. Because the paper fails Criterion 3 (no empirical evidence/methods), both decision and plain_criterion2_decision are exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05). Although Footnote 1 notes that fieldwork was conducted within a broader 2011-2014 ANR research project and p. 539 makes a single passing reference to field surveys ('Les enquêtes de terrain montrent...'), the article is a narrative institutional and policy overview with no empirical methods section, no description of study sites, sample size, interviewees, survey instruments, or analytical procedures, and no primary qualitative or quantitative data. All quantitative figures and local examples are drawn from legislative texts and secondary grey-literature reports (e.g., PN-AEPA 2012, Zoungrana 2011, Valfrey-Visser et al. 2012, Diallo 2009, Charpentier 2011), and the paper is not a systematic empirical synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Unclear: the paper cites secondary national water-access and equipment-functionality statistics from PN-AEPA and NGO reports (e.g., 58.5% rural and 80% urban access in 2011; PEM and AEPS functionality rates) and asserts without quantitative data that the two regions managed by ADAE have the highest functionality rates, while its AUE analysis focuses primarily on organizational roles and internal participation rather than empirically measured household or community access outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5: while the national policy exposure (2000 Reform, municipal decentralization, tariff and delegation rules, AUEs) in Burkina Faso is described at a macro-institutional level, the paper reports no identifiable empirical study design, no empirical sample or study sites, and no primary outcome measurement linking exposure to access.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in French (with bilingual French/English title and abstract). Per Inclusion Criterion 10, translation from the provided French full text is feasible, so the record is not excluded on language grounds.

study_design: not reported (narrative institutional and policy overview)
population_and_sample: not reported (macro-institutional overview of rural and semi-urban drinking-water governance in Burkina Faso; no empirical study sample or sites reported)
exposure: 2000 rural and semi-urban drinking-water sector reform (Decree 2000-514), municipal decentralization (Law 055-2004/AN and Decree 2009-107), local tariff/cost-recovery rules, and delegated affermage vs. licensed Water Users Associations (AUE)
outcome: Secondary national drinking-water coverage and infrastructure functionality rates (from PN-AEPA/NGO reports) and qualitative institutional/participation dynamics within AUEs (no primary empirical access outcome reported)
rationale: Baron and Bonnassieux (2013) examine drinking-water service governance in rural and semi-urban Burkina Faso (C1=yes) and discuss rule-type legal and regulatory mechanisms directly governing access—including municipal ownership transfer, delegated affermage vs. licensed Water Users Associations (AUE), and volumetric/flat-rate tariff rules (C2=yes under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading). However, the article is a narrative institutional and policy overview rather than an empirical study or systematic synthesis: despite a footnote acknowledging fieldwork under a broader 2011-2014 ANR grant and a passing mention of field surveys, the paper reports no empirical methodology, no study sites, sample, or data-collection procedures, and no primary empirical evidence, relying instead on legislative texts and secondary grey-literature reports (C3=no, C5=no). Excluded as E05 (no empirical evidence).
